_note: Curated 'Happening now' items for the Natarta Stay safe guide. Each item is written in Natarta's own words from an official public source (linked, dated). Keep it calm: no fear words, no politics. Schema is checked by feed/build-feed.mjs; the Action signs it into happening.json.

items.title: Fake health plan sites during Open Enrollment
what: Open Enrollment for Medicare and Marketplace plans is a busy time, and fake plan sites show up with it.
Some pay to appear at the top of search results and use look-alike web addresses and logos.
signs: A search result marked "Ad" or "Sponsored" that looks official
A web address close to Medicare.gov or HealthCare.gov, but not quite
Pressure to sign up on the phone today
actions: Type Medicare.gov or HealthCare.gov yourself, or call Medicare at 800-633-4227.
Scroll past ads and look for the .gov ending.
Report anything odd at ReportFraud.ftc.gov.

items.title: Fake QR codes on parking meters
what: People have found QR stickers placed over the real codes on parking meters.
Scanning one can open a look-alike payment page that asks for your card.
signs: A sticker that sits on top of another code
A link with spelling mistakes or swapped letters
A page that asks for card details right away
actions: Pay at the meter or in the city's official parking app.
Preview the link first. Natarta's Scan shows where a code goes.
Already entered details? Change that password and check your card statement.

items.title: Copied car dealership websites
what: Some websites copy a real dealer's logos, listings and photos, sometimes with AI.
They ask buyers to pay upfront for a car that never arrives.
signs: A rare or hard-to-find car at a great price
Payment by wire transfer only, before you see the car
No in-person visit or independent inspection allowed
actions: Search the dealer's name with words like "review" or "complaint".
Ask to see the car in person, or hire an inspection service.
Walk away from upfront, wire-only payment.

items.title: Postcards about extra veterans benefits
what: Veterans are getting postcards about a "Veterans Savings Program" that offers extra monthly money.
That program doesn't exist. The postcard wants you to call and give personal or bank details.
signs: A program name the VA has never mentioned to you
"Call right away or miss out"
Real benefit names used to make it look official
actions: Don't call the number on the postcard.
Questions about benefits? Call the VA Benefits Hotline at 1-800-827-1000.
Report it at ReportFraud.ftc.gov or VSAFE.gov.

items.title: Packages you never ordered
what: Some people are getting cheap, random items they didn't order. Sellers do this to post fake reviews in your name.
Some packages include a QR code that leads to a sign-in page built to collect passwords.
signs: A package addressed to you that you didn't order
Something small and random inside, like seeds or wipes
A note saying "scan to see who sent this" or "scan to return"
actions: You don't have to pay for it or send it back.
Don't scan the QR code inside.
Change your shopping passwords and check your credit free at AnnualCreditReport.com.

items.title: Look-alike bill payment sites in search results
what: When you search for a company to pay a bill, the top result can be a paid ad from a different business.
You might pay extra fees, or pay someone who isn't your provider.
signs: An "Ad" or "Sponsored" label next to the result
A site name that's a little different from your provider's
Extra "service" fees at checkout
actions: Type your provider's website yourself, or use the address on your bill.
Scroll past paid ads in search results.
Pay in the company's own app when you can.

items.title: "Learn to trade" coaches on social media
what: Social media is full of trading coaches showing off fancy cars and trips.
Trading is risky, and no one can promise big returns with little risk.
signs: Guaranteed profits or "no risk"
Luxury photos used as proof it works
Pressure to join fast or bring in friends
actions: Search the name with words like "review" or "complaint".
Look up anyone selling investments at Investor.gov.
Take your time and talk it over with someone who has your back.
